Canada operates one of the world's most comprehensive federal and provincial fiscal incentive frameworks for industrial research and development, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under section 37, section 127, and section 127.1 of the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX (section 2900 to section 2903) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945)1.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most significant structural reform since 2012–20147. Following announcements in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the 2025 Federal Budget, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026), retroactively enhancing the federal SR&ED program for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024)7. Specifically, the legislation doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (surpassing the $4.5 million interim proposal in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective 3-year average annual revenue phase-out calculation under subsection 127(10.6), extended the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 20242.

Furthermore, the 2026 Federal Budget proposed expanding the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026 to cover specified commercialisation expenditures—including regulatory approval or certification costs and intellectual property (IP) protection expenses—while the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process in April 2026 for businesses with under $25 million in gross business income8. At the provincial level, Québec replaced its legacy R&D wage and partnership credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, with the consolidated Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), offering a 30% refundable credit on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess spending9.
Section 1: Statutory Architecture and Technological Eligibility Under Subsection 248(1)
1.1 Legislative Foundation and Evolution of CRA Administrative Guidance

The statutory gateway to all federal and harmonised provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act18. Under this provision, SR&ED means systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that is undertaken in one of three primary categories—basic research, applied research, or experimental development—alongside eight enumerated categories of directly supporting work, while explicitly excluding seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activities19.

While the statutory language of subsection 248(1) has remained stable since the 1990s, the administrative framework used by the Canada Revenue Agency to evaluate technical eligibility has evolved through four distinct historical stages18:

items: Pre-1985 Era (Interpretation Bulletin IT-439): Prior to 1985, Revenue Canada relied on Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 to interpret "applied or basic research" and "development" under the Income Tax Regulations18. Taxpayer feedback demonstrated that IT-439 failed to adequately explain the eligible scope of industrial research and development18.

1985–1994 Era (Introduction of "Experimental Development" and IC 86-4): In the May 1985 Federal Budget Papers, the Department of Finance announced amendments to the regulatory definition of scientific research to introduce the term "experimental development," clarifying that projects involving only routine engineering or routine development were excluded18. On March 4, 1986, the Department of Finance confirmed to Revenue Canada that qualifying work must embody scientific or technological advancement, contain elements of scientific or technological uncertainty, and be conducted in a systematic and organised fashion18. This led to the publication of Information Circular 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development) in 1986 (and its third revision, IC 86-4R3, in 1994), establishing the three foundational criteria of scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content18. In 1992, the definition of experimental development was further refined to emphasize that work must be experimental in nature and undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new or improve existing materials, devices, products, or processes18.

1998–2021 Era (Northwest Hydraulic and the Five Questions): In May 1998, Judge Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada issued the landmark decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839), synthesizing IC 86-4R3 and subsection 248(1) into a five-part judicial approach (subsequently summarized as five questions by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393)18. The CRA codified these five questions in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012 and revised in 2015)18.

2021–Present Era (The Two Requirements — "Why" and "How"): In August 2021, following modernization consultations started in 2020 to simplify the claimant experience, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and published the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives18. The 2021 Guidelines consolidated the five questions into two overarching requirements: the "Why" Requirement (purpose of the work) and the "How" Requirement (methodology of the work)18. Both the five questions and the two requirements derive directly from subsection 248(1) without altering the underlying legal standard18.

body.text: 1.2 Detailed Analysis of the Two Requirements ("Why" and "How")
The "Why" Requirement: Advancement and Uncertainty

To satisfy the "Why" requirement under paragraphs 248(1)(a) through (c), the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement19. In CRA administrative practice, the hallmark of eligible advancement is the generation or discovery of conceptual knowledge—such as new scientific theories, principles, predictive models, or systemic technological relationships—rather than mere factual knowledge, such as routine measurements, empirical observations, or parameter tabulations19. Whether a claimant categorizes the sought-after knowledge as "scientific" or "technological" is not legally determinative, as both satisfy the statute19.

New scientific or technological knowledge is required only when the claimant encounters a scientific or technological uncertainty—defined as a situation where it is unknown or uncertain whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency or limitation in the available scientific or technological knowledge base19. The baseline of available knowledge comprises both the internal knowledge and experience of the claimant's business (its competent professionals and proprietary know-how) and publicly accessible knowledge and standard practice in the relevant field globally19.

Crucially, if a technical obstacle is circumvented using a workaround based on known methods or standard engineering practice, or if the knowledge is simply acquired externally by hiring consultants, training personnel, or purchasing proprietary technology, the work does not resolve the underlying technological uncertainty and fails the "Why" requirement19. Conversely, because subsection 248(1) looks to the purpose for which the work is undertaken, a project that fails to achieve its technical or commercial goals—or that proves a hypothesis false—still satisfies the "Why" requirement, as the elimination of a viable technological pathway advances the knowledge base19.
The "How" Requirement: Systematic Investigation or Search

To satisfy the "How" requirement, the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis19. Merely executing work in an organised, methodical, or professional manner using established engineering design protocols, standard software development lifecycles, or routine troubleshooting does not constitute a systematic investigation for SR&ED purposes19. Rather, the CRA requires the presence of four sequential methodological elements19:

items: Formulation of a Hypothesis: Generating a specific idea or proposition, consistent with known scientific or technological facts, that serves as a starting point for further investigation aimed at resolving the identified uncertainty19.

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Subjecting the hypothesis to structured physical or digital experiments (such as building and instrumenting experimental prototypes, pilot plants, or test rigs) or rigorous mathematical, engineering, or computational analysis (such as finite element analysis, algorithmic complexity modelling, or statistical correlation)19. As testing progresses, initial hypotheses may evolve or be modified into subsequent hypotheses19.

Logical Conclusions: Analysing the experimental or analytical results to determine why a specific test succeeded or failed and formulating logical conclusions regarding the underlying scientific or technological relationships19.

Contemporaneous Evidence: Maintaining dated records, logs, commit histories, test data, photographs, or physical artifacts generated as the work progressed to substantiate each iteration of the investigation19.

body.text: 1.3 Categories of Eligible SR&ED Work

Subsection 248(1) divides qualifying SR&ED activities into three core research and development categories under paragraphs (a), (b), and (c), alongside one derivative category for support work under paragraph (d)19. Basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view19. While historically concentrated in universities, non-profit institutions, and government laboratories, basic research is also merged into business research across sectors such as biotechnology, nanotechnology, advanced materials science, and computer applications, with results typically published in scientific journals19. Applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b) is similarly undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge, but with a specific practical application in view19. For example, whereas studying a newly discovered virus to understand its molecular characteristics is basic research, investigating how to develop a vaccine against that virus using those identified characteristics constitutes applied research19.

Experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto9. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of Canadian industrial SR&ED claims, such as scaling up and optimizing processes for large-scale manufacturing19. According to the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work, technological uncertainty in experimental development typically arises when a claimant attempts to achieve specific features or functions while restricted by constraints where existing technological knowledge is inadequate19. The CRA recognizes seven primary indicators of insufficient technological knowledge: existing design methods are inapplicable; specifications do not conform to existing standards; too many interacting variables or unknowns are present; operating parameters fall outside normal ranges; the nature of the problem evolves dynamically; baseline data is not readily available; or interlocking system constraints (including economic or cost targets where standard methods fail) prevent a routine solution19.

Support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight enumerated activities: (i) engineering, (ii) design, (iii) operations research, (iv) mathematical analysis, (v) computer programming, (vi) data collection, (vii) testing, and (viii) psychological research19. Support work does not qualify as SR&ED in isolation; it is eligible if and only if it satisfies a strict two-prong statutory test: it must be commensurate with the needs (corresponding in amount, size, extent, or duration to what is strictly necessary) and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada19. Notably, while research in the social sciences or humanities is generally excluded under paragraph 248(1)(g), psychological research into mind and behaviour functions is explicitly permitted under paragraph 248(1)(d)(viii) when it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of an eligible SR&ED project in the physical sciences or technology19.
1.4 Explicitly Excluded Work and Production Run Boundaries
Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the Income Tax Act establish an absolute statutory exclusion for seven categories of work, even if conducted alongside an R&D project19:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion19.
Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes19.
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities19.
Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas19.
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process19.
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes (such as aesthetic or cosmetic redesigns lacking technological uncertainty)19.
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection (unless directly in support of and commensurate with core SR&ED under paragraph (d))19.

body.text: When experimental development takes place within a commercial manufacturing facility ("shop-floor SR&ED"), the CRA enforces strict delineation rules under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy29. The CRA classifies shop-floor trials into two contexts: ED+EP (Experimental Development resulting in Experimental Production, where a trial run is conducted solely for experimentation and no commercial run would otherwise have occurred) and ED+CP (Experimental Development conducted simultaneously or in conjunction with Commercial Production—the default classification unless ED+EP is demonstrated)29. Any output beyond the minimum quantity reasonable and necessary to test the hypothesis is classified as excess production; all labour, material, and overhead costs attributable to excess production or normal commercial production (CP) must be carved out and excluded from the SR&ED claim29. Furthermore, the eligibility of a project ceases on its completion date, defined as the earliest point at which the technological advancement is achieved by resolving the associated uncertainties, the uncertainties are determined to be unresolvable, or the project is terminated for any reason36.
Section 2: Federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Mechanics — Pool of Deductible Expenditures and Investment Tax Credits
2.1 The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Subsection 37(1))

The first pillar of the federal SR&ED program is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures governed by subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act and detailed in the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy (updated March 27, 2026)36. Rather than requiring taxpayers to deduct current R&D expenses in the year incurred under section 9 or capitalize and depreciate them under paragraph 20(1)(a), subsection 37(1) aggregates allowable SR&ED expenditures into a cumulative, running tax pool37. A taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct any portion (from 0% to 100%) of the positive balance remaining in its subsection 37(1) pool at the end of a taxation year against its business income for that year37. Any undeducted balance in the subsection 37(1) pool carries forward indefinitely to future taxation years without expiration36.

body.text: Three critical structural rules govern the subsection 37(1) pool. First, because the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is a notional calculation under Regulation 2900(4) and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) is depreciated under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8, neither the PPA nor the capital cost of SUE enters the subsection 37(1) pool14. Second, under subsection 37(4) and Regulation 2902(c), no deduction is permitted under subsection 37(1) for expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (such as purchasing a patent or technology licence), and under subsection 37(5), if a payment qualifies as both an SR&ED expenditure and a charitable gift under section 110.1 or 118.1, it must be deducted under section 37 and cannot be claimed as a charitable donation37. Third, when a corporation undergoes a loss restriction event (an acquisition of control, or a change in majority-interest beneficiary for a trust), a deemed taxation year-end is triggered immediately before the event and the subsection 37(1) pool is reduced to nil under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1)37. The undeducted pre-acquisition pool balance can only be reinstated and carried forward in subsequent taxation years if the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and the deduction is limited to the corporation's income for the year (before taking the subsection 37(1) deduction) from that same business or a similar business4.
2.2 SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Phase-Out Formulas

The second pillar of the federal SR&ED program is the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) and the Refundable Investment Tax Credit under section 127.1, as detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026)2. All corporations (including large private corporations, foreign-controlled corporations, and public corporations that do not qualify as ECPCs or that spend above their expenditure limit), individuals, trusts, and partnerships earn a basic federal ITC of 15% on their SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year (less any provincial super-allowance benefit amount)2. Qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an enhanced ITC rate of 35% (comprising the 15% basic rate under subsection 127(9) plus a 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1)) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit2. Qualified expenditures exceeding the annual expenditure limit earn the 15% basic rate2.

Following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the maximum annual Expenditure Limit doubled from $3,000,000 (for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, available to CCPCs only) to $6,000,000 (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, available to both CCPCs and ECPCs), prorated for short taxation years of less than 51 weeks based on the number of days in the taxation year2. Associated CCPCs must share the annual expenditure limit and allocate it using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) pursuant to subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3), while ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group must share and allocate the $6 million limit across the consolidated group2.

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit was phased out linearly when the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year fell between $10,000,000 and $50,000,0002: Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is less than or equal to $10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $10,000,000.
For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out under one of two statutory methods2:

items: Default Taxable Capital Method (CCPCs Only — Subsection 127(10.2)): The $6,000,000 limit begins to phase out when the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated (reduced to nil) when taxable capital reaches $75,000,0002. Every $10 of taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1: Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000.

body.text: In this formula, A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is less than or equal to $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,0002.

items: Revenue Phase-Out Method (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs — Subsection 127(10.6)): Because public corporations frequently carry high balance-sheet share capital that would penalize them under a taxable capital test, subsection 127(10.6) requires Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—and permits CCPCs (provided all associated CCPCs in a group file a joint election on the prescribed form)—to calculate the phase-out of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit using the average annual revenue of the preceding 3 fiscal years as reflected in their financial statements (or based on the actual number of fiscal years if the corporation has fewer than 3 fiscal years)2. Under the revenue method, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when 3-year average annual revenue reaches $15,000,000 and becomes nil at $75,000,000 or greater2. For associated CCPCs electing the revenue method, the calculation must sum the financial statement revenues of all group members across the 3 preceding fiscal years (regardless of whether they were associated throughout that entire 3-year period), include each corporation's reasonable share of partnership or trust revenues, and apply reasonable adjustments for intra-group sales of goods or services so that the revenue reflects a single economic entity2. For consolidated ECPCs, the annual revenue on the group's consolidated financial statements is used2.

body.text: 2.3 Refundability Rules: Qualifying Corporations, Excluded Corporations, and ECPCs

Under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, whether an unused SR&ED ITC can be refunded in cash (rather than carried back 3 years or carried forward 20 years to offset Part I tax payable) depends on the claimant's legal classification and whether the expenditure is current or capital2.

A CCPC is defined as a Qualifying Corporation under subsection 127.1(2) if its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year, calculated before specified future tax consequences such as loss carrybacks) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit2. The Qualifying Income Limit starts at $500,000 and phases out based on prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada2. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $500,000 Qualifying Income Limit phased out linearly between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of taxable capital2: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000,

where A is nil if taxable capital is $10,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $10,000,0002. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $500,000 Qualifying Income Limit phases out linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 of taxable capital2: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000,

where A is nil if taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,0002. When a CCPC's taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 (or $50,000,000 for pre-December 16, 2024 years), both its Qualifying Income Limit and its Expenditure Limit are reduced to zero, extinguishing all entitlement to refundable ITCs2.

body.text: Crucial Partnership Structural Trap (Subsection 127(8))

As confirmed in the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy and Tax Court jurisprudence (All Colour Chemicals Ltd. v. The Queen), a partnership is not a "person" or a CCPC12. Because subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(8) calculate the SR&ED deduction and the ITC at the partnership level as if the partnership were a separate person—and a partnership cannot maintain a carryforward pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures—the ITC earned by a partnership is limited to the 15% basic rate12. Furthermore, when that 15% ITC is allocated to a CCPC partner under subsection 127(8), none of the allocated ITC is refundable to the CCPC unless it is a qualifying corporation (only partners that are qualifying corporations, individuals, or certain trusts may access a 40% refund rate)2. In addition, salary or wages paid to a partner are treated as a distribution of partnership income rather than deductible employment remuneration and cannot be claimed as SR&ED wages, and "specified members" (passive or limited partners not actively, regularly, and continuously engaged in the partnership's business) are prohibited from claiming SR&ED ITC allocations or limited partnership SR&ED losses12. In contrast, participants in a joint venture (which is not a partnership) file their own independent SR&ED claims directly on their respective shares of expenditures, preserving CCPC 35% enhanced refundable ITC entitlement12.
Carryback, Carryforward, and Deemed Deduction Rules

Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs (or refundable ITCs that a claimant elects not to have refunded) may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years and carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years under subsection 127(5) to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable2. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash to a claimant in a taxation year is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable in that year, thereby reducing the ITC available for carryforward or carryback and triggering an equivalent reduction to the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e)2.
Section 3: Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) vs. Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B))

A claimant must select either the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method on Form T661 (Lines 160 and 162 in Part 1) for each taxation year34. Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, the election to use the Proxy Method must be made when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year; if no election is made, the Traditional Method applies automatically34. Once Form T661 has been filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that taxation year, though a claimant may switch methods in subsequent taxation years34.

Under the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations), the claimant identifies, tracks, substantiates, and allocates its actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures that are directly attributable (directly related and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED in Canada34. Both these actual overhead expenditures and the salaries of support/supervisory employees not directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED (claimed on Line 360 of Form T661) are added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures and included in qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn ITCs34.

Under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations), the claimant does not specifically track or claim actual overhead or non-directly-engaged support salaries on Form T661 (instead deducting those actual expenses as ordinary business deductions under section 9 of the Income Tax Act)34. In their place, when calculating qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes, the claimant adds a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of its eligible SR&ED salary base34.

To illustrate the financial divergence between the two methods, consider the official example in Section 6.10 of the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, where a Qualifying CCPC incurs $100,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries (all forming part of the salary base), $15,000 in materials consumed, and $50,000 in actual directly related and incremental SR&ED overhead34. Under the Traditional Method, allowable SR&ED expenditures added to the subsection 37(1) pool equal $100,000 + $15,000 + $50,000 = $165,000; the PPA is $0, yielding total qualified SR&ED expenditures of $165,000 and a 35% federal ITC of $57,75034. Under the Proxy Method, allowable SR&ED expenditures added to the subsection 37(1) pool equal $100,000 + $15,000 = $115,000 (while the $50,000 of actual overhead is deducted as an ordinary business expense under section 9); the PPA equals $100,000 × 55% = $55,000, yielding total qualified SR&ED expenditures of $115,000 + $55,000 = $170,000 and a 35% federal ITC of $59,500—generating an additional $1,750 in refundable tax credits without the administrative burden of tracking overhead34.
3.2 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Mechanics, Specified Employee Caps, and YMPE Limits

As set out in the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated March 27, 2026) and subsections 2900(4) to 2900(10) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 as 55% of the claimant's Salary Base, subject to specified employee limitations and an overall business expenditure cap42.
Composition of the Salary Base and Mandatory Exclusions (Regulation 2900(5) and 2900(9))

The Salary Base comprises the portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (plus permissible foreign SR&ED wages under subsection 37(1.4)) incurred and paid in the taxation year or within 180 days after the end of the taxation year42. Under Regulation 2900(5), if an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED for All or Substantially All (ASA — 90% or more) of their employment time, 100% of their eligible salary is deemed to be directly engaged in SR&ED29. However, under Regulation 2900(9), the following five items must be strictly excluded from the Salary Base for all employees (both regular and specified employees)3:

items: Taxable benefits included in employment income under section 6 of the Income Tax Act3.
Stock option benefits under section 7 of the Income Tax Act3.

Unpaid remuneration from a prior taxation year that was paid in the current taxation year and deemed incurred under subsection 78(4) (Line 310 of Form T661), as well as unpaid vacation pay or salary deferral arrangements deemed paid3.
Bonuses3.
Remuneration based on profits42.

body.text: Employer-paid related benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, EHT, and pension contributions) are also excluded because they do not meet the definition of "salary or wages" under subsection 248(1)38.
Dual Statutory Caps on "Specified Employees" (Subsection 37(9) and Regulation 2900(7))

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, a specified employee of a claimant is an employee who is either a specified shareholder of the employer—defined as a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or any related corporation—or a person who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (for example, a spouse, child, sibling, or parent of a controlling shareholder)28. Specified employees are subject to two distinct statutory ceilings tied to the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan38.

First, under the Direct SR&ED Expenditure Cap (Subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1)), for any specified employee (under both the Traditional and Proxy methods), bonuses and remuneration based on profits are 100% disallowed as SR&ED expenditures38. Furthermore, the maximum base salary or wages of a specified employee that can be claimed as an allowable SR&ED expenditure (on Line 305/306 of Form T661) cannot exceed 5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual is a specified employee38: Maximum Direct SR&ED Salary Claim = 5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee ÷ 365).

Second, under the Proxy Salary Base Restriction (Regulation 2900(7) and 2900(8)), when calculating the Salary Base for the 55% PPA in Part 5 (Section A, Lines 850–860) of Form T661, the amount included for each specified employee is further restricted to the lesser of two statutory limits: 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary or wages for the year (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, after excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid amounts paid in the year); or 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the total number of days the claimant employed the individual in the taxation year (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee)41: Maximum Proxy Salary Base Inclusion = lesser of (75% × eligible salary or wages) and (2.5 × YMPE × number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is an employee of the claimant ÷ 365).

Under Regulation 2900(8) and subsection 37(9.3), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the aggregate amount included across all associated corporations cannot exceed the single 5 × YMPE direct expenditure cap and the single 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base cap, which must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED)42.

For the direct SR&ED wage deduction on Line 305, 100% of the $220,000 qualifies because ASA applies and $220,000 is below the $373,000 (5 × YMPE) ceiling34. Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(6))

To ensure that the notional 55% PPA plus claimed SR&ED and specific statutory deductions do not exceed the claimant's actual total business outlays for the taxation year, Regulation 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA42: Maximum PPA = A − (B + C).

In this formula, A represents the total of all amounts deducted in computing the claimant's net income from the business for the year for tax purposes (including Cost of Goods Sold); B represents the total of all deductions claimed in computing business income for the year under section 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance, interest expense, and bad debts), section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), section 26 (banks), section 30 (land improvements for farming), section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), section 37 (deductible SR&ED expenditures claimed), sections 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration and development expenses), and section 104 (trusts); and C represents total expenditures incurred in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building (building rent or lease expense)42. In practice, as noted by the CRA, the Overall Cap does not restrict the PPA if the claimant carries on a diversified business or has deducted more than $55 of eligible non-SR&ED general operating expenses (excluding building rent, CCA, and interest) for every $100 of SR&ED salary in its Salary Base42.
3.3 Detailed Eligibility Rules by Expenditure Category
1. SR&ED Salary or Wages (Subsections 248(1), 37(8), 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 78(4))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), eligible salaries or wages must constitute employment income under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Income Tax Act (reported on a T4 slip)38. Dividends, shareholder draws, consulting fees paid to independent contractors, and partnership distributions are not salary or wages12. For non-specified employees, base salary, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, and taxable benefits under section 6 are eligible to the extent attributable to SR&ED38. Non-cash taxable benefits qualify only if their value is a reasonable estimate of actual employer cost, excludes GST/HST or PST for which an Input Tax Credit (deemed government assistance under subsection 248(16)) can be claimed, and is not otherwise deducted as a business expense38. Stock option benefits under section 7 (excluded after November 14, 2005, following Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149) and extended vacation, maternity/parental, or long-term sick leave are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages28.

Under the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4)), any salary, wages, or bonus accrued in a taxation year that remains unpaid on the 180th day after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, and is instead deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (provided it was reported on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year accrued and claimed on Line 310 in the year paid)28. A payment made on the 180th day satisfies the time limit38. Reasonable vacation or holiday pay and deferred amounts under a statutory salary deferral arrangement are deemed paid even if unpaid on the 180th day, though they remain excluded from the Proxy Salary Base38.

While subsection 37(2) generally restricts foreign R&D expenses to an ordinary income deduction (ineligible for the subsection 37(1) pool or ITCs), subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) deem permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada to be incurred in Canada if all five statutory conditions are met4:

items: The foreign SR&ED work was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (work performed by a subcontractor outside Canada never qualifies)38.
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred38.
The work related to a business of the claimant4.
The foreign work was an integral part and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant4.
The salary or wages were not subject to income or profits tax in another country38.

body.text: The permissible foreign salary amount (allocated between regular employees on Line 307 and specified employees on Line 309 of Form T661) is limited to the lesser of actual eligible foreign SR&ED wages (Amount A) or 10% of total Canadian SR&ED salaries and wages claimed on Line 306 (Amount B), such that Line 307 + Line 309 ≤ 0.10 × Line 30638. Associated travel, hotel, and meal expenses for foreign SR&ED work do not qualify as SR&ED overhead46.
2. Materials for SR&ED (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) & Regulation 2900(2)(a))

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), materials qualify at 100% under both the Traditional and Proxy methods on Line 325 of Form T661 only when they are consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada36. To constitute "materials for SR&ED," the items must be physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or components (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible thing on which the SR&ED is performed or that results from the SR&ED29. Laboratory glassware (petri dishes, beakers, pipettes), cleaning supplies, general utilities (electricity, water, natural gas), lubricants, and storage media (CDs/DVDs) do not compose the body of the experimental object and cannot be claimed as materials on Line 325 (though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method)58.

Materials are consumed when they are destroyed, absorbed, broken down, or rendered virtually valueless (retaining less than 10% of their original cost in scrap value) as a result of the SR&ED39. Materials are transformed when they are changed or incorporated into another material, prototype, custom product, or commercial asset during SR&ED while retaining economic value29. Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed during SR&ED—never in an earlier year when merely purchased, delivered, or transferred out of inventory39. For purchased materials (from Canadian or foreign suppliers), eligible cost is the GAAP "laid-down cost" (invoice price plus customs/excise duties, freight, and storage)58. For internally manufactured inventory subsequently consumed or transformed in SR&ED, cost includes laid-down raw materials, direct production labour, and the GAAP share of production overhead—even if the claimant has elected the Proxy Method for its SR&ED claim58.
3. Contract Expenditures and Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii) & Subsection 127(9))

Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 27, 2026) and Third-Party Payments Policy, external R&D expenditures are governed by strict arm's-length, look-through, and right-to-exploit rules24. When a claimant contracts an arm's-length taxable supplier (a Canadian resident person or Canadian partnership, or a non-resident operating through a Canadian permanent establishment) to perform Basic Research, Applied Research, Experimental Development, or paragraph 248(1)(d) Support Work in Canada where the payer controls the work and retains exclusive ownership of the results, 100% of the current contract expenditure enters the subsection 37(1) pool, and 80% qualifies for federal ITCs under subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9)1. Under subsection 127(26), if an arm's-length contract invoice remains unpaid 180 days after year-end, the entire 80% qualified portion is deducted from qualified expenditures in that year and added back (at 80%) only in the year paid47. Under subsections 37(14) and 37(15) (the look-through rule), where a contractor incurs non-qualifying capital expenditures embedded in the contract price, the performer must notify the payer in writing without delay upon request or within 90 days after calendar year-end of the required contract reduction40.

In contrast, payments to a non-arm's-length (NAL) contractor for SR&ED are deductible in the payer's subsection 37(1) pool, but yield 0% qualified expenditures to the payer for ITC purposes39. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures (which are not reduced by the intercompany contract payment) or transfers those qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the NAL payer by filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13)14. When goods or non-SR&ED services are purchased from a NAL supplier, subsection 127(11.6) limits the qualified expenditure to the adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost (stripping out all intercompany profit markups)29. Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24), interposing an arm's-length intermediary between two NAL parties to manufacture a qualified contract expenditure is nullified57.

For Third-Party Payments, payments made to external research bodies where the performer controls the research and results are generally published—provided the SR&ED is carried on in Canada, relates to the claimant's business, and the claimant obtains an entitlement to exploit the results (such as a preferential right to early or pre-publication findings before they enter the public domain)—are 100% deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool and 80% eligible for ITCs39. The CRA classifies recipients into A Entities (Canadian resident corporations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1), claimed on an accrual basis in the year SR&ED is performed) and B to F Entities (approved associations [B], approved universities, colleges, and research institutes [C], paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporations [D and F], and granting councils such as NSERC, CIHR, and SSHRC [E] under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii), claimed on a cash basis in the year paid and reported on Form T661 and Form T1263)43.
4. Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures, SUE, and equipment lease costs were completely excluded from SR&ED incentives5. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA issued three updated policy documents—the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8 / June 22, 2026), and the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026)—governing property acquired or lease costs incurred after December 15, 20245.

Under the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (Line 390 and Part 6B of Form T661), depreciable property (other than land, buildings, or leasehold interests in buildings excluded under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e)) acquired after December 15, 2024, that becomes available for use (subsections 37(1.2) and 13(27)) in the taxation year qualifies for 100% inclusion in the subsection 37(1) pool and 100% inclusion in qualified expenditures for ITCs if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that either the property would be used during All or Substantially All (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or ASA (90% or more) of its value would be consumed in SR&ED in Canada14. Capital cost includes purchase price, installation, freight, and customs/excise duties14. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) cannot be claimed14. Furthermore, used depreciable property qualifies for the subsection 37(1) pool deduction on Line 390, but is a prescribed exclusion from ITCs under Regulation 2902(b) and must be deducted on Line 53214. Any asset claimed on Line 390 is deemed to have claimed 100% CCA and must not be added to Schedule T2SCH814.

Under the Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) Policy (Line 504 and Part 6C of Form T661), if new depreciable property (never previously used or rented for any purpose, and excluding buildings, GPOEF, and Prescribed Depreciable Property [PDP] under Regulation 2900(11) intended for commercial plant construction/commissioning and primary commercial use) is acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, and does not meet the ≥90% ASA intention test, it qualifies as SUE if its actual operating time in SR&ED in Canada is primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) during two statutory windows29. First-Term SUE is measured from the date the property is available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that date, deeming 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowed money interest under section 21 and adjusted for NAL costs under subsection 127(11.6)) to be a qualified SR&ED expenditure for ITC purposes14. Second-Term SUE applies provided the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and is measured from the date of acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that date, deeming an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (for a cumulative 50% across both terms) to be a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes14. The capital cost of SUE does not enter the subsection 37(1) pool and is instead depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8 (with the UCC reduced in the following year by the ITC claimed or refunded)14.

Under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, for equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, claimants using the Traditional Method claim 100% as a direct lease cost if the equipment is used ASA (≥90%) in SR&ED, or claim the proportional SR&ED usage percentage on Line 360 as overhead if used <90% (provided it is directly related and incremental)5. Claimants using the Proxy Method (excluding GPOEF) claim 100% of the lease cost if used ASA (≥90%), 50% of the lease cost if used primarily (>50% to <90%) in SR&ED, and 0% if used ≤50%5. Dedicated bandwidth leased for SR&ED (not GPOEF) qualifies under the Proxy Method pursuant to Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen5. Rent for a building is strictly excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e) unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903 approved by the Department of Finance3.
5. Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and subsections 127(27) through 127(36), if a claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use a property (or another property incorporating that property)—including materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, SUE, or contract-developed physical assets—within 20 taxation years of acquiring the property (extended from 10 years by subsection 127(36)), the previously earned ITC is recaptured and added directly to Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion59. The recapture amount equals the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property, or the original ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (for an arm's-length sale) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property at the time of conversion to commercial use or NAL disposition59.

Three key exceptions mitigate ITC recapture. First, under the In-House Labour and Overhead Exemption, if a claimant manufactures a prototype or commercial asset in-house, only the cost of purchased physical components or materials transformed is subject to recapture; in-house SR&ED salaries and overhead are never recaptured (whereas ordering a fabricated module from an arm's-length supplier subjects the entire supplier invoice price to recapture)59. Second, under the De Minimis (<10%) Rule, no recapture applies if scrap proceeds or the FMV upon commercial conversion is less than 10% of the property's original cost59. Third, under the Intellectual Property Exemption, selling or licensing IP arising from SR&ED never triggers ITC recapture57. Any ITC recaptured in a taxation year is added back to the claimant's subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2)37.
Section 4: Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Federal Grant Stacking
4.1 Statutory Reduction Rules for Assistance and Contract Payments

To prevent double-dipping on the same dollar of R&D expenditure, paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) and 127(19) of the Income Tax Act require claimants to reduce their subsection 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures and their qualified SR&ED expenditures (on Lines 513 to 517 of Form T661) by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has "received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive" on or before the filing-due date of the income tax return for the taxation year10.

Under subsection 127(9), government assistance encompasses assistance from any federal, provincial, territorial, municipal, or foreign government, Crown corporation, or public authority (including non-profit organisations funded by government), whether in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, investment allowance, or provincial/territorial R&D tax credit (excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself)10. Non-government assistance is defined as any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance received from a private entity for an outlay or expense that would otherwise be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x)10. Contract payments encompass amounts payable to an SR&ED performer by an arm's-length taxable supplier, a Canadian government/public authority, or a tax-exempt entity for SR&ED performed for or on its behalf10. As established in Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 773), a commercial fixed-price contract to deliver a functional product where the vendor bears the financial and technical risk is ordinary business revenue rather than a "contract payment" for SR&ED, unless the contract explicitly or implicitly obligates the vendor to perform SR&ED on the customer's behalf22.

A critical accounting distinction applies to provincial tax credits attributable to the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)10. Under the Proxy Method, a portion of a provincial R&D tax credit (such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit or BC SR&ED Tax Credit) is earned on the notional 55% PPA10. As explained in Section 4.5 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, the entire provincial tax credit (including the PPA portion) reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) for ITC purposes10. However, because the PPA is not in the subsection 37(1) pool, the portion of the provincial tax credit attributable to the PPA does not reduce the subsection 37(1) pool under paragraph 37(1)(d); instead, that specific portion must be included directly in net income for tax purposes on Schedule T2SCH1 under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the taxation year it is received10. Similarly, under Québec's R&D regime, any portion of a Québec R&D credit earned on support salaries that are excluded from federal Proxy claims does not reduce the subsection 37(1) pool and is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) when received10.
4.2 Stacking Federal Innovation Grants and Clean Economy ITCs with SR&ED

Canadian businesses frequently combine ("stack") non-dilutive direct innovation grants and Clean Economy ITCs with SR&ED tax credits61. The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is Canada's premier direct R&D grant program for incorporated, profit-oriented small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent employees63. Administered through a network of Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs), standard IRAP provides non-repayable cost-shared financial contributions covering up to 80% of internal technical salaries and subcontractor costs for pre-approved R&D projects (with typical awards ranging from $75,000–$200,000 for initial projects up to $1 million–$4 million+ for larger streams, alongside specialized streams such as IRAP AI Assist and the NRC IRAP Clean Technology Initiative, which received a $298 million 3-year renewal in the 2026 Federal Budget)8. Unlike SR&ED, IRAP requires pre-approval before costs are incurred61. For SR&ED purposes, IRAP reimbursements reduce the direct SR&ED expenditure base dollar-for-dollar on Line 515 of Form T661, but they do not reduce the Salary Base used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)41.

To see the mathematical mechanics of stacking NRC IRAP with SR&ED under the Proxy Method, suppose a Qualifying CCPC incurs $250,000 in directly engaged SR&ED engineer salaries and receives an 80% NRC IRAP grant ($200,000)61. The claimant's net out-of-pocket direct salary cost is $250,000 − $200,000 = $50,00061. However, under Regulation 2900(4), the 55% PPA is calculated on the gross unreduced SR&ED salary base of $250,000, generating a PPA of $250,000 × 55% = $137,50034. Thus, total qualified SR&ED expenditures after deducting the $200,000 IRAP assistance equal $250,000 + $137,500 − $200,000 = $187,50041. At the 35% enhanced federal ITC rate (before provincial credits), the company earns $187,500 × 35% = $65,625 in federal SR&ED refunds on top of the $200,000 IRAP grant—recovering $265,625 against its $250,000 direct cash payroll outlay (thereby covering direct wages plus a portion of employer overhead and related benefits)2.

For large-scale capital and R&D projects, the Strategic Response Fund (formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund — SIF), administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) (originally launched in 2017 as the Strategic Innovation Fund and strengthened in the 2026 Federal Budget with an additional $1 billion over six years starting in 2028–29), supports major industrial R&D, commercialization, and capital scale-up projects—typically with total project costs of $10 million or more8. Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and the Federal Court of Appeal decision in CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178), both non-repayable contributions and conditionally or unconditionally repayable government loans/contributions (such as SIF/Strategic Response Fund contributions) provided in respect of SR&ED constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures in the year received or receivable, with the subsection 37(1) pool and ITC restored under paragraph 37(1)(c) only as repayments are actually made in future years10.

Finally, under sections 127.44 to 127.491 of the Income Tax Act, Canada offers refundable Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits (such as the 30% Clean Technology ITC and the Clean Electricity ITC) on clean energy and decarbonization equipment1. A taxpayer cannot claim both an SR&ED ITC and a Clean Economy ITC on the exact same dollar of capital equipment cost; however, as noted in clean technology grant stacking guidelines, a company can route its R&D labour, materials, and PPA overhead to the 35% SR&ED ITC while routing its commercial clean energy equipment acquisitions to the 30% Clean Technology ITC within the same project and taxation year61.

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive Jurisdictional Analysis: Québec's New CRIC Regime vs. Ontario and Western Provinces
1. Québec: Transition to the Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)

In its March 25, 2025 Budget Speech, the Québec Ministry of Finance enacted a sweeping overhaul of provincial innovation taxation9. For taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished its four legacy R&D tax credits—the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V), the Tax Credit for University Research or Public Research Centres (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, though cumulative consortium fee balances at the end of a taxation year ending after March 25, 2025, remain claimable until December 31, 2029)—and replaced them with the single, unified Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)9.

The CRIC is restricted exclusively to corporations (or corporations that are members of a partnership) operating a business in Québec with an establishment in Québec; unlike the legacy R&D wage credit, individuals and trusts cannot claim the CRIC9. In addition to traditional Basic Research, Applied Research, and Experimental Development (whose technical definition remains harmonised with federal subsection 248(1) and is audited scientifically by the CRA), the CRIC expands eligibility to pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec as a continuation of or in conjunction with Québec R&D conducted by or on behalf of the corporation9. Eligible pre-commercialization work includes tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for initial marketing approval or certification; product design (including development of form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and selection of materials); and implementing a quality control system strictly required for initial regulatory approval or certification9.

The CRIC qualified expenditure base consists of 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees for Québec R&D or pre-commercialization; 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for work performed in Québec; 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, research consortium, or university entity in Québec; and 100% of property acquisition costs (capital expenditures) incurred for R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec, excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings (provided the property is not also claimed under another Québec credit such as C3i or a Large Investment Project tax holiday)9. Québec does not use the federal 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount9. To focus assistance on higher-value-added jobs, a corporation's qualified expenditures must exceed an annual Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000, or the sum of the basic personal amount under the applicable personal income tax system for each employee, prorated by the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities9. The CRIC provides a 30% refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold—available regardless of the corporation's total assets (eliminating the legacy $50 million to $75 million asset phase-out)—and a 20% refundable tax credit on all qualified expenditures above the $1,000,000 limit (up from the legacy 14% basic rate)9. Claimants must file Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures), Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization — Codes 112 and 113), Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (Allocation Agreement among associated corporations for the $1 million limit), and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (Pre-Commercialization Component Information)9.
2. Ontario: Three-Tier Credit Architecture and Capital Cost Nuances

Ontario maintains three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA10. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule T2SCH566) is an 8% refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario (maximum annual refund of $240,000, shared among associated corporations)7. Ontario has not increased its $3 million expenditure limit to match the federal $6 million limit, and retains its own stricter phase-out thresholds: the $3 million limit phases out linearly when prior-year federal taxable income of the associated group is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year specified capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,00068. With respect to capital expenditures, a November 2026 advisory analysis by TechHelp Canada notes that Ontario announced in its 2026 Fall Economic Statement that Bill C-15's Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, automatically restored capital expenditure eligibility (for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024) across both the ORDTC and OITC (adding over $50 million in provincial relief over three years)7; however, an October 2026 tax analysis by Copoint and the CRA's July 17, 2026 OITC guidance webpage observe that published CRA instructions for Schedule T2SCH566 still describe the OITC base as "100% of current expenditures" and have not yet confirmed the addition of restored capital costs to the refundable OITC base68.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule T2SCH508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (after deducting any OITC and OBRITC claimed), with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward7. A corporation may waive or renounce the OITC (under subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007) or ORDTC on or before the filing-due date if it wishes to avoid reducing its federal subsection 37(1) pool and federal 35% ITC base10. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules T2SCH568 and T2SCH569) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible research contract with an Ontario Eligible Research Institute (ERI, such as an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institute), up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (yielding up to $4,000,000 in annual refunds), provided no connected employee of the claimant is remunerated by the ERI under the contract67.
3. British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan

Among the western provinces, British Columbia (Form T666) is the only jurisdiction that has fully harmonised with every element of the 2024–2026 federal SR&ED reforms68. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, BC increased its 10% refundable tax credit expenditure limit from $3 million to $6,000,000 (maximum $600,000 refundable credit), expanded the taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), restored capital expenditures, and permanently extended the credit by removing its statutory expiry date under BC Budget 202667.

In Alberta (AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970), the province replaced its former 10% SR&ED tax credit effective January 1, 2021, with the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act67. The IEG provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's "base level of spending" (defined as the average of the corporation's qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the immediately preceding 2 taxation years) plus an enhanced 20% refundable payment (the 8% base plus a 12% incremental bonus) on eligible R&D spending exceeding that 2-year average base, up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $4,000,000 (phased out between $10 million and $50 million of taxable capital)67. Updated guidance issued by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration on June 30, 2026, confirmed that while IEG claims continue to rely on revised federal Form T661 line reporting, Alberta retains its $4 million cap and did not adopt wholesale federal capital expenditure restoration68.

In Saskatchewan (Schedule T2SCH403), for qualifying SR&ED expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, the province doubled the expenditure threshold for its 10% refundable CCPC credit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (yielding up to $200,000 in cash refunds), while maintaining a 10% non-refundable credit for non-CCPCs and CCPC spending above $2,000,000, subject to an overall combined annual tax credit cap of $1,000,000 ($10,000,000 in expenditures)67.
Section 6: Governing Bodies, Statutory Filing Procedures, Form T661 Architecture, and the CRA Audit Process
6.1 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the Absolute 18-Month Bar

Under subsection 37(11) (for deducting SR&ED expenditures in the subsection 37(1) pool) and paragraph 127(9)(m) (for earning SR&ED Investment Tax Credits) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred36.

Under subsection 37(11.1), subsection 37(12), and subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, this statutory reporting deadline is absolute43. Following the November 17, 2005 legislative amendment to subsection 220(2.2) (which overrode the earlier Federal Court decision in Alex Parallel Computers Research Inc. v. Canada, 1998), the Minister of National Revenue has no statutory authority to extend the SR&ED reporting deadline or accept late-filed prescribed forms or project narratives under the taxpayer relief provisions, regardless of extenuating circumstances28. If a claimant fails to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing all prescribed line items by the deadline, the expenditures are permanently barred from entering the subsection 37(1) pool and permanently lose all entitlement to federal and harmonised provincial SR&ED ITCs (though current expenses may still be reclassified and deducted as ordinary business expenses under general provisions of the Income Tax Act)43.

body.text: 6.3 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 2026)

As announced in the 2025 Federal Budget and implemented by the CRA in April 2026 (with updated procedural guidance issued October 14, 2026), businesses can apply for optional Pre-Claim Approval before starting an SR&ED project (or shortly after starting work, before incurring significant costs) to obtain upfront technical assurance from the CRA that their planned work meets SR&ED eligibility requirements11. To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the business must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership; have gross business income of less than $25,000,000; and be in good standing with the CRA15. Furthermore, the proposed project must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under litigation15.
The application workflow follows three sequential steps15:
