body.text: Once the taxation year ends and the formal Form T661 claim is submitted, pre-claim approved projects that undergo an expenditure-only review benefit from an accelerated CRA service standard of 90 calendar days (compared to 180 calendar days for standard reviewed claims)30.
6.4 CRA Review Procedures, Service Standards, Gross Negligence Penalties, and Appeals

For claims accepted as filed without a review, the CRA targets processing within 60 calendar days13. Under the CRA's published service standards (The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, updated April 20, 2026), refundable claims generally have an overall processing standard of 120 calendar days (or 180 calendar days when selected for a detailed technical and financial review, which the CRA targets meeting 90% of the time), while claimant-requested adjustments to refundable claims have a 240-calendar-day standard and non-refundable claims or adjustments have a 365-calendar-day target30.

Once a claim is selected for review (via automated risk assessment, AI-assisted screening introduced in 2026, or random sampling), the claim cannot be withdrawn and the Part 10 certification cannot be revoked11. The review is conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) and reports to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who audits expenditure allowability and prepares a Financial Review Report [FRR] under the supervision of a Financial Review Manager [FRM])30. Reviews follow a three-step process: (1) Initial telephone contact and a formal Request for Information letter (typically providing 30 days to respond) with a meeting agenda; (2) The Review Meeting (conducted virtually via videoconference by default, or on-site upon exceptional case-by-case approval by the review management team), featuring direct interviews with the hands-on personnel who performed or supervised the work, a virtual or physical premises tour, examination of dated contemporaneous evidence indicated on Lines 270–282 of Form T661, and communication of preliminary findings; and (3) Issuance of the formal written SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and Financial Review proposal package30.

Under Section 5.10.0 of the CRA Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, RTAs are strictly forbidden from negotiating eligibility with claimants21. An RTA must never propose accepting certain projects in exchange for the claimant withdrawing other projects, nor allow an arbitrary percentage of a project or unsubstantiated overhead without an objective factual basis21. Conversely, under David Ludmer et al. v. MNR (93 DTC 1351), The Queen v. McKinley Transport Ltd. (90 DTC 6243), and AGT Ltd. v. Canada (97 DTC 5189), CRA reviewers possess broad statutory authority under section 231.1 and subsection 230(1) of the Income Tax Act to expand the scope of a review beyond the initial review plan and compel production of potentially relevant documents21.

Under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes a false statement or omission on an original or amended SR&ED claim, the CRA bears the statutory burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the overstatement resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act24. When established, the penalty under subsection 163(2) applies to both the understated Part I tax payable and 100% of the overstated refundable ITC claimed, with the CRA deeming the overstated ITC to have been deducted prior to any legitimate ITCs available in the pool80. In cases of deliberate fabrication or false representation of dates and documents, criminal prosecution can result in court-ordered fines of 150% to 300% of the amount claimed (R. v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684; Tempora, SCC 2018)28.

If a disagreement arises during a review, the claimant is encouraged to escalate concerns informally to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) or Financial Review Manager (FRM)30. Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has a strict statutory deadline of 90 days from the date on the Notice to file a formal Notice of Objection (online via My Business Account / Represent a Client or by mail using Form RC592) with the Chief of Appeals at the designated CRA Appeals Intake Centre30. While general taxpayers do not have to pay disputed tax or penalties during an objection (though normal interest accrues on any balance ultimately found owing), a Large Corporation (defined as having total taxable capital employed in Canada together with related corporations exceeding $10,000,000 at the end of the taxation year) must reasonably describe each issue, specify the exact dollar relief sought for each issue in its Notice of Objection, and pay 50% of the disputed tax amount during the dispute30. If differences cannot be resolved with the CRA Appeals Officer, the claimant may appeal the assessment or reassessment to the Tax Court of Canada30.
Section 7: Landmark Canadian SR&ED Case Law and Judicial Precedents (1988–2026)
Canadian jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) plays a decisive role in interpreting subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 12720.
7.1 Foundational Jurisprudence on the Definition of SR&ED and Routine Engineering

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC, May 1, 1998), the taxpayer conducted five physical hydraulic scale-modelling projects relating to river flow, dam spillways, and sediment transport22. Judge Bowman allowed four of the five projects, establishing the foundational judicial framework for interpreting "experimental development" under paragraph 248(1)(c)18. Judge Bowman articulated the five criteria (subsequently summarized as five questions by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393): (1) technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; (2) formulation of hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; (3) a procedure consistent with the total discipline of the scientific method, including formulating, testing, and modifying hypotheses; (4) a resulting technological advancement; and (5) a detailed record of hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed20. Critically, Northwest Hydraulic established the doctrine of system uncertainty, holding that technological uncertainty and advancement can exist even when all individual components are known technologies, provided their interaction within a complex integrated system is uncertain28.

Decided a decade earlier shortly after "experimental development" was introduced into the Regulations, Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC, May 9, 1988) established the enduring legal boundary between SR&ED and routine engineering: work that applies techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field does not qualify as SR&ED21. The Tax Court held that systematic investigation requires trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, rather than mere trial-and-error adjustments during equipment fabrication20. Subsequently, in Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 1081 (TCC, September 15, 1999), the Tax Court confirmed that the rejection or disproving of a hypothesis is itself a technological advancement because it eliminates an uncertain technical avenue and adds to the body of technological knowledge22.

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (January 17, 2017), the appellant developed a motorized hydraulic system to control the descent speed of a theatre fire curtain to replace traditional counterweights22. The Tax Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the challenges were resolved through routine engineering27. While defining a hypothesis simply as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial," the Court emphasized that in mature fields like applied mechanics, standard engineering practice is broad; the fact that none of the appellant's personnel held engineering degrees or formal technical diplomas in mechanical or hydraulic design—and that no external hydraulic specialists were engaged—weighed heavily against finding that the problem exceeded the capabilities of a competent professional in the field20.
7.2 Evidentiary Standards: Contemporaneous Documentation vs. Credible Oral Testimony

A recurring issue in SR&ED audits is whether the absence of contemporaneous written records is automatically fatal under Question 5 / Step 4 of the "How" requirement20. In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA, December 21, 1998), the Federal Court of Appeal reversed the Tax Court's blanket denial of an SR&ED claim where a key engineer had died prior to trial and written test records were sparse20. While affirming that repeatability and evidence of testing are essential (and that merely producing a final product or patent does not prove how it was developed), the FCA held that documentary evidence is not strictly mandatory as a matter of law if the taxpayer provides a plausible explanation for why documents are unavailable and adduces credible oral or circumstantial evidence establishing that systematic testing occurred20.

Similarly, in 116736 Ontario Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1816 (TCC, June 9, 1998), where a fire destroyed the claimant's supporting records, the Tax Court accepted oral testimony "not without hesitation" because extenuating circumstances existed and the testifying inventor had an established track record of commercialized R&D21. Likewise, in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, the Tax Court allowed four process development projects despite minimal paperwork because the witness testimony was found to be "highly credible"22. Nevertheless, as the CRA emphasizes in Chapter 5 of the Claim Review Manual, taxpayers lacking dated contemporaneous evidence place themselves in a "very precarious position"21.
7.3 Software, Information Technology, and Industrial Control Jurisprudence (2015–2026)

In ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 263 / 2016 TCC 50, the Tax Court allowed the software developer's SR&ED claim (and awarded legal costs in 2016 TCC 50) for work undertaken to increase system stability in an electronic health record architecture where no existing methods were available22. Conversely, in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (aff'd 2022 FCA 72), where the claimant developed a dynamic SQL database software tool ("PTS-Project"), both the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal28. Although the Tax Court accepted that the claimant formulated valid hypotheses, the claim failed on the remaining criteria because the taxpayer retained only a single final code base and could not demonstrate systematic testing or intermediate iterations28. On appeal (2022 FCA 72), the Federal Court of Appeal also affirmed strict rules on expert witnesses, holding that an expert has an overriding duty to assist the court impartially and cannot be used to establish unproved factual methodologies "through the back door"86.

More recently, in Dazzm Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129 (October 8, 2024), the Tax Court delivered a significant victory for modern software SR&ED22. The claimant developed a cloud-based SaaS platform integrating open-source tools (including React and Redux) and encountered severe performance bottlenecks28. The Tax Court allowed the appeal in full, holding that systemic uncertainty in integrating open-source software frameworks goes beyond routine debugging or optimization when standard approaches fail, and reinforced the use of performance metrics and developer testimony to prove systematic investigation28. In Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7, the Tax Court issued a split decision on two industrial control software projects: the Court allowed the MTCLM SIL 4 train-control box project on the basis of cumulative "system uncertainty" not resolvable by available methods, but disallowed $1,293,692 on the SCADACOM-5 upgrade project, holding that modernizing and scaling up software using known tools is routine product development rather than experimental development28.
7.4 Food Science, Manufacturing, Fraud, and Filing Deadline Jurisprudence (2011–2026)

In the food manufacturing sector, Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 35 (July 26, 2023) addressed a custom frozen pie manufacturer that appealed the CRA's denial of $343,449 in SR&ED expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs across projects between 2013 and 2016 aimed at reducing sodium and fat, extending shelf life to 21 days without preservatives, and maintaining crust integrity after freezing20. Justice Lafleur ruled in favour of Canafric on six projects, holding that business and economic constraints are relevant factors when considering technological uncertainty, and that eliminating failed recipe iterations via systematic analysis and credible oral testimony constituted technological advancement20. Similarly, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. (2025 TCC), the Court allowed an SR&ED claim for developing shelf-stable cold-pressed juice ("Chrisoda") using novel high-pressure processing (HPP), because hypotheses were systematically tested via measurable pH and microbial count observations28. Conversely, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 183, the Tax Court denied 13 food processing projects (2005–2009) because the claimant engaged in unrecorded trial-and-error, reconstructed narratives after the fact, and arbitrarily split estimated wages evenly across production batches28.

In heavy manufacturing and energy engineering, Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18 (February 6, 2023) allowed a tractor design claim because the manufacturer clearly demonstrated system-level integration uncertainties22, whereas Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63 (May 2, 2025) (mobile direct-contact water heaters for fracking) and Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King (September 25, 2025 TCC) (roller-compacted concrete field processes) dismissed the appeals as unsystematic trial-and-error prototyping with vague hypotheses and poor records22.

On compliance, fraud, and statute-barred years, Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173 resulted in a split decision: while the Tax Court allowed certain 2007–2008 industrial heating element projects on their technical merits, it upheld the CRA's reopening of statute-barred taxation years (2006 and 2009) and imposition of penalties because the claimant's T661 technical reports contained plagiarized text copied from supplier websites—constituting a misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred years28. Finally, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (aff'd 2011 FCA 355), Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 211 (aff'd 2016 FCA 301), and Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 9 (aff'd 2018 FCA 57), the Federal Court of Appeal and Tax Court consistently held that the 18-month reporting deadline under subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m) is mandatory and absolute: failing to file Schedule T2SCH31 alongside Form T661 (Easy Way Cattle), or having a related corporation file the project descriptions instead of the actual claimant (Westsource), permanently extinguishes the SR&ED claim after 18 months22.
